1. Core Clinical Tension: A 23-year-old woman presents with life-threatening massive hemoptysis ('five cups filled with blood') against a 3-month history of subacute constitutional symptoms (cough, weight loss, night sweats). While over 90% of massive hemoptysis cases in cavitary disease originate from hypertrophied bronchial circulation, this presentation involves a low-pressure pulmonary artery branch aneurysm (Rasmussen aneurysm) requiring targeted angiography and endovascular embolization.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission phase includes emergency resuscitation, documentation of hemorrhagic shock (BP 100/60 mmHg, Hb 6 g/dL requiring transfusion of 4 units PRBCs), and initial plain chest radiography showing bilateral cavitary lesions, stopping strictly prior to sputum acid-fast bacilli smear, CT imaging, and invasive angiography.
3. Differential Distinctions: Common sources like bronchial artery neovascularization or pyogenic bacterial lung abscesses are differentiated by selective arteriography and microbiological smear; identifying acid-fast bacilli together with pulmonary angiography confirms a tuberculous Rasmussen aneurysm.
case_prompt: A 23-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a one-day history of coughing up approximately five cups filled with blood. For the preceding 3 months, she had been experiencing a persistent cough, significant weight loss, and drenching night sweats. On examination, she appears diaphoretic and in severe distress. Her blood pressure is 100/60 mmHg, and triage blood analysis reveals profound anemia with a hemoglobin level of 6 g/dL. She is urgently resuscitated with fluid support and transfused with 4 units of packed red blood cells, which raises her hemoglobin to 10 g/dL. Plain chest radiography demonstrates multiple cavitary lesions distributed throughout both lungs.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Bronchial arterial hypertrophy represents the primary source of massive hemoptysis in cavitary lung disease, but selective bronchial angiography demonstrated normal vessels without active contrast extravasation.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The bronchial arteries were not enlarged, and no active contrast extravasation was detected from them.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Pyogenic Lung Abscess / Cavitary Bacterial Pneumonia
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: While pyogenic cavitary lung abscess can produce chronic constitutional symptoms and cavitation, the etiology was verified as mycobacterial by positive acid-fast bacilli staining.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Chest X-ray revealed active pulmonary tuberculosis with multiple cavities in both lungs. Sputum was positive for acid-fast bacilli.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Diagnostic Pivot: Pulmonary Artery (Rasmussen) Aneurysm secondary to Tuberculosis
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Contrast CT demonstrated focal parenchymal enhancement, and selective pulmonary angiography definitively identified a 5-cm pulmonary artery aneurysm originating from the left lower lobe, which was successfully treated with coil embolization.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: A 5 cm diameter oval aneurysm was detected originating from the left lower lobe posterior-medial segment pulmonary artery (Figure 1(c))... A single Gianturco steel coil 5 mm in diameter was selectively placed at the neck of the aneurysm with occlusion of the pulmonary aneurysm
